implementation_notes: JavaScript cannot keep client code secret, so the rule is the platform's own posture: use the reviewed primitives the runtime ships - crypto.subtle (SubtleCrypto) in browsers and Node, or node:crypto (OpenSSL wrappers) on the server - and let keys live in non-extractable CryptoKey or KeyObject form where possible. MDN's own warning is the design note made concrete: the primitives "are easy to misuse", and "secure key management and overall security system design are extremely hard to get right", so the mechanism must be standard (AES-GCM, HMAC, PBKDF2, ECDSA with named curves) while any "clever" client-side scheme - an obfuscated algorithm, a secret in the bundle, base64 called encryption - is security by obscurity. Server-side checks, not hidden client logic, are what protect a browser app.
pitfalls: Anything shipped to a browser is readable: minification is not encryption, and a secret key or "hidden" API credential in the bundle is public - CWE-656's client-side example.

crypto.getRandomValues and crypto.subtle require a secure context (HTTPS) and Node's WebCrypto is asynchronous; falling back to Math.random for compatibility silently produces predictable keys and nonces.
Raw keys can be exported and copied around the heap: prefer non-extractable CryptoKey objects in the browser and keep server secrets server-side.
